q: At a shop counter, the cashier passes each packet over a device that reads the black-and-white stripes printed on it. Which input device is this?
x: A barcode reader shines light on the printed bars and reads the product code from them. An optical mark reader senses filled-in circles on answer sheets, not product stripes.

q: A shopkeeper saves the day's sales file on a USB drive so that he can use it again next week. Which stage of the information-processing cycle is this?
x: Keeping data or results on a device for later use is the storage stage. Processing would be working out totals from the sales, which is not what saving the file does.

q: A teacher wants the whole class to see her computer screen enlarged on a white wall. Which output device should she use?
x: A multimedia projector takes the computer's display output and throws a large image on a wall or screen. A scanner and a web camera are input devices, and a printer gives paper output.

q: A student who cannot use a keyboard gives commands to the computer by speaking. Which input device picks up his voice?
x: A microphone turns sound into signals the computer can accept, so it is an input device. A speaker does the opposite: it is an output device that produces sound.

q: Which statement about a compiler and an interpreter is correct?
o: An interpreter translates the whole program first; a compiler translates and runs one statement at a time
A compiler translates assembly language only; an interpreter translates machine language only
Both translate the whole program first and differ only in the speed of the computer they need
A compiler translates the whole program first; an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time
x: A compiler converts the complete source program into machine code before it runs, while an interpreter takes one statement, translates it, executes it, then moves on. The reversed statement swaps the two definitions.

q: A hospital pays a software house to write a program designed only for its own patient-record system. Such software is called:
x: Software written to order for one particular user or organisation is custom-built (tailor-made). Packaged software is ready-made and sold to many users, like a common word processor.

q: Which of the following is a low-level language?
x: Assembly language uses short codes (mnemonics) that match machine instructions one to one, so it is a low-level language. Python, Java and BASIC are high-level languages written in English-like statements.

q: Banks read the account and cheque numbers printed in special magnetic ink at the bottom of cheques with which device?
x: MICR reads characters printed with ink containing magnetic particles, which is why banks use it for cheques. An OMR only senses whether marks are present in fixed positions; it does not read magnetic characters.

q: A printed page is scanned, and the computer then turns the picture of the text into characters that can be edited in a word processor. Which technology does this?
x: OCR software recognises the shapes of letters in a scanned image and converts them into editable text. OMR only detects marks in set places, such as filled circles, and cannot read ordinary printed words.

q: Which of the following is a non-impact printer?
x: A laser printer forms the image with a laser and toner, with nothing striking the paper, so it is non-impact. Dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and drum line printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper, so they are impact printers.

q: Which statement best describes the role of the operating system?
o: It is an application program used mainly for typing letters and reports
It is a hardware chip that stores the user's documents permanently
It manages the hardware and provides a platform on which application programs run
It translates programs written in a high-level language into machine code
x: The operating system is system software that controls memory, devices and files, and application programs run on top of it. Translating high-level programs is the job of a compiler or interpreter, not the operating system itself.

q: Ayesha wants to keep records of 500 library books and search them quickly by author or title. Which kind of application software suits this job best?
x: A database program stores records in fields and lets the user search and sort them, for example by author. A word processor can hold a list of books but cannot search and sort records as a database does.

q: Which list puts the languages in order from lowest level (closest to the hardware) to highest level?
o: Assembly language, machine language, high-level language
High-level language, assembly language, machine language
Machine language, high-level language, assembly language
Machine language, assembly language, high-level language
x: Machine language is binary code the CPU runs directly, assembly language replaces it with mnemonics, and high-level languages use English-like statements. Putting assembly below machine language reverses the first two levels.

q: A weather office records 500 temperature readings and works out "Average this week: 31 °C". Later, the weekly averages of a whole year are used to draw a yearly chart. Which statement is correct?
o: The weekly average is data only, because it is a number
The 500 readings are information, because they were measured carefully
The yearly chart is data, because it was made from averages
The weekly average is information, and it becomes data for making the yearly chart
x: Processed, meaningful results are information, but information from one process can be the data (input) of the next, as the weekly averages are for the yearly chart. A value is not data just because it is a number; what matters is whether it has been processed into a useful result.

q: A program is written in the machine language of one type of processor. What usually happens if it is moved to a computer whose processor has a different instruction set?
o: It runs there unchanged, because machine language is the same on all computers
It runs there after it is passed through a compiler once more
It runs there only if the second computer has more memory
It will not run there without being rewritten for that processor
x: Machine language is machine-dependent: its binary codes are the instructions of one processor family, so another instruction set will not understand them. A compiler translates high-level source code, not machine code, so recompiling the machine-code program does not help.

q: The system bus of a computer is made up of which three buses?
o: Data bus, address bus and control bus
Data bus, power bus and memory bus
Address bus, serial bus and input bus
Control bus, cache bus and output bus
x: The system bus joins the CPU, memory and input/output and consists of the data bus, address bus and control bus. Power, cache, serial and output buses are not the three standard parts.

q: In a microcomputer, the whole CPU is built on a single chip. This chip is called a:
x: A microprocessor is a CPU made on one integrated-circuit chip. The motherboard is the main circuit board on which the microprocessor and other parts are mounted, not the CPU chip itself.

q: A quad-core processor has:
o: Four processing cores on one chip
Four times as much RAM as normal
x: "Quad" means four: a quad-core processor has four cores, each able to execute instructions, in a single processor package. The number of cores says nothing about disks or RAM.

q: Which of the following travels on the data bus?
o: The address of the memory location to be read
A 'memory write' signal from the control unit
An instruction being read from memory into the CPU
The ticks of the system clock
x: The data bus carries the data and instructions themselves between the CPU, memory and input/output. The address goes on the address bus, and read/write and timing signals go on the control bus.

q: Registers inside the CPU that a program can use to hold data and intermediate results of any operation are called:
x: General-purpose registers hold data and partial results for many kinds of operation. The program counter, instruction register and MAR each have one fixed special job: next instruction address, current instruction and memory address.

q: Which of the following tasks is NOT done by the control unit?
o: Directing data between the CPU parts
x: Arithmetic such as adding is carried out by the ALU. The control unit decodes instructions, sends control and timing signals and directs the flow of data, but it does not do the calculation itself.

q: For the instruction ADD, during which step of the instruction cycle does the ALU actually add the two numbers?
x: The instruction is first fetched from memory, then decoded so the control unit knows it means ADD; the adding happens in the execute step. In the decode step the operation is only identified, not carried out.

q: A program is saved on the hard disk. Before the CPU can run its instructions, the program must first be:
x: The CPU fetches instructions from main memory, so the program is first copied from the disk into RAM. ROM is read-only and holds fixed start-up instructions; programs are not copied into it to be run.

q: An 8-bit data bus is used to bring a 32-bit number from memory. What is the smallest number of transfers needed?
x: Each transfer carries 8 bits, so 32 ÷ 8 = 4 transfers are needed. One transfer would only be enough if the bus were 32 bits wide.

q: In a machine instruction such as ADD R1, R2, the part ADD that tells the CPU which operation to perform is called the:
x: The opcode names the operation, here addition. R1 and R2 are the operands: the data or registers the operation works on.

q: A bus in a computer is best described as:
o: A set of parallel lines that carry signals between components
A program that moves files between folders
A storage area that keeps data when power is off
A device that converts digital signals to analogue
x: A bus is a group of parallel wires or lines on which signals travel between the CPU, memory and input/output. A device that converts digital to analogue signals is a modem, not a bus.

q: A CPU's address bus is made one line wider, from 16 lines to 17 lines. What happens to the number of memory locations it can address?
x: With n address lines the CPU can address 2ⁿ locations, and 2¹⁷ = 2 × 2¹⁶, so the number doubles. Adding one line does not add one location; it adds a whole new bit position.

q: Which statement about the address bus and the data bus is correct?
o: The data bus width sets how many locations can be reached; the address bus width sets how many bits move at once
Both widths only decide the clock speed of the processor
The address bus width sets how many locations can be reached; the data bus width sets how many bits move at once
The address bus carries the data and the data bus carries the addresses
x: More address lines give more distinct addresses (2ⁿ locations), while more data lines carry more bits in each transfer. The swapped statement mixes up the two buses' jobs.

q: During the fetch step, the address in the memory address register goes to memory, and the instruction comes back to the memory data register. Which buses are used for these two movements, in that order?
x: The address travels from the MAR to memory on the address bus, and the instruction read from that location travels back to the MDR on the data bus. The control bus only carries signals such as 'memory read', not the address or the instruction.

q: A processor runs at 2 GHz and each instruction takes 4 clock cycles. How many instructions can it complete in one second?
x: 2 GHz is 2,000,000,000 cycles per second, and 2,000,000,000 ÷ 4 = 500,000,000 instructions. Multiplying instead of dividing gives the wrong 8 billion.

q: When a computer is switched on, the first start-up instructions (such as the BIOS) are read from a memory that keeps them without power. This memory is:
x: ROM is non-volatile and holds fixed start-up instructions that are needed every time the computer is turned on. RAM, cache and registers lose their contents when the power goes off.

q: Which storage device uses flash memory and has no moving parts?
x: An SSD stores data in flash memory chips, so nothing spins or moves. A hard disk has spinning platters and moving heads, and tape and DVD drives also have moving parts.

q: Taking 1 TB = 1,024 GB, a 1 TB hard disk holds how many gigabytes?
x: Each step up from GB to TB is a factor of 1,024, so 1 TB = 1,024 GB. 1,000,000 is close to 1,024 × 1,024, the number of megabytes in 1 TB, not gigabytes.

q: Which type of ROM is supplied blank and can be programmed by the user only once?
x: PROM (programmable ROM) can be written once and then cannot be changed. EPROM and EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed, and mask ROM is written by the maker during manufacture, not by the user.

q: Why does a computer need secondary storage even though it has RAM?
o: RAM is slower than secondary storage, so programs run from the disk
RAM can only store numbers, while secondary storage can store text
RAM is volatile and limited, while secondary storage keeps data permanently
Secondary storage is needed only to start the computer each time
x: RAM loses its contents when power is off and is smaller, so files must be kept on secondary storage such as a hard disk. RAM is actually much faster than secondary storage, not slower.

q: The CPU needs a piece of data and does not find it in the cache. What happens next?
o: It reads the data from main memory, which takes longer
It stops the program with an error message
It reads the data from ROM instead
It waits until the data appears in the cache by itself
x: A cache miss means the data is fetched from the slower main memory (RAM), and a copy is usually kept in cache for next time. It is not an error, and ROM does not hold the program's working data.

q: When RAM is full, the operating system uses part of the hard disk as if it were extra RAM. This is called:
x: Virtual memory lets the operating system move parts of programs between RAM and a space on the disk, so more can run than RAM alone allows. Cache memory is a small fast memory between the CPU and RAM, not space on the disk.

q: Which list puts these optical discs in order of their usual storage capacity, smallest first?
x: A CD holds about 700 MB, a single-layer DVD about 4.7 GB and a single-layer Blu-ray disc about 25 GB. Blu-ray uses a shorter-wavelength laser, so it packs more data than a DVD.

q: Which pair correctly matches a storage device with the way its data is read?
o: CD-ROM: a magnetic head; hard disk: a laser beam
CD-ROM: a laser beam; hard disk: a magnetic read/write head
CD-ROM: an electric charge in cells; hard disk: a laser beam
CD-ROM: a magnetic head; hard disk: an electric charge in cells
x: Optical discs such as CD-ROMs are read by a laser that detects pits and lands; a hard disk is read by heads that sense magnetised spots. Electric charge in cells is how flash memory stores data, not either of these.

q: Saima is editing a large report. She saved it to the hard disk an hour ago and has made changes since. The power suddenly fails. What is lost?
o: Only the changes made since the last save, which were in RAM
The whole report, including the copy saved on the hard disk
Nothing, because RAM keeps data without power
Only the copy on the hard disk, while RAM keeps the changes
x: Unsaved changes are held in volatile RAM and are lost, but the hard disk is non-volatile, so the version saved an hour ago remains. RAM does not keep data when power fails.

q: Moving down the memory hierarchy from registers to cache to RAM to hard disk, which statement is true?
o: Capacity, speed and cost per byte all increase
Capacity decreases while speed and cost per byte increase
Capacity increases while speed and cost per byte decrease
Speed increases while capacity and cost per byte decrease
x: Registers are the fastest and most expensive per byte but tiny; each lower level is slower and cheaper per byte but much larger. That is why a computer has only a few registers but a disk of hundreds of gigabytes.

q: Which statement about CD-R and CD-RW discs is correct?
o: A CD-R can be erased and rewritten; a CD-RW can be written only once
Both can only be read, because both are kinds of CD-ROM
Both can be rewritten, but a CD-RW holds ten times more data
A CD-R can be written only once; a CD-RW can be erased and rewritten many times
x: R stands for recordable (write once, then read) and RW for rewritable (erase and write again). The swapped statement reverses the meanings of the two letters.

q: Which digit can NOT appear in an octal number?
x: Octal is base 8, so it uses only the digits 0 to 7; the digit 8 is not allowed. 7 is the largest valid octal digit.

q: When binary is converted to octal by grouping, each octal digit stands for a group of how many bits?
x: 8 = 2³, so each octal digit matches exactly 3 bits. Groups of 4 bits are used for hexadecimal, because 16 = 2⁴.

q: In the binary number (10010110)₂, the leftmost bit, which has the highest place value, is called the:
x: The leftmost bit has the largest place value (here 2⁷ = 128), so it is the most significant bit. The rightmost bit, with place value 1, is the least significant bit.

q: What is the largest decimal value that can be written with three hexadecimal digits?
x: The largest is (FFF)₁₆ = 15×256 + 15×16 + 15 = 3,840 + 240 + 15 = 4,095, which is 16³ − 1. 4,096 is the count of different values (0 to 4,095), not the largest one.

q: Counting in octal, which number comes immediately after (777)₈?
x: Adding 1 to 7 in octal gives 0 carry 1 in every place, so (777)₈ + 1 = (1000)₈; in decimal 511 + 1 = 512 = 8³. (778)₈ and (800)₈ contain the digit 8, which octal does not have.

q: A 0 is added to the right end of an unsigned binary number, so (1011)₂ becomes (10110)₂. What happens to its value?
x: Every bit moves one place left, so each place value is doubled: (1011)₂ = 11 becomes (10110)₂ = 22. Adding a 0 on the left, not the right, would leave the value unchanged.

q: In the octal number (5372)₈, what is the decimal value of the digit 3 in its place?
x: From the right the places are 8⁰ = 1, 8¹ = 8, 8² = 64, 8³ = 512; the 3 is in the 64s place, so it is worth 3 × 64 = 192. 24 would be 3 × 8, the next place to the right.

q: What is the product (101)₂ × (11)₂?
x: (101)₂ = 5 and (11)₂ = 3, and 5 × 3 = 15 = (1111)₂. By shifting: 101 + 1010 = 1111, giving the same answer.

q: Using 8-bit 2's complement, how is the decimal number −5 written?
x: +5 is 00000101; inverting every bit gives 11111010 (the 1's complement), and adding 1 gives 11111011. 10000101 is the sign-and-magnitude form, not 2's complement.

q: What is (9A)₁₆ + (27)₁₆?
x: A + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17 = 16 + 1, so write 1 and carry 1; then 9 + 2 + 1 = 12 = C, giving (C1)₁₆. Check in decimal: 154 + 39 = 193 = 12×16 + 1; (B1)₁₆ forgets the carry.

q: Which of the following is equal to (110110)₂?
x: (110110)₂ = 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 54; grouping in threes, 110 110 gives (66)₈ = 6×8 + 6 = 54. (54)₈ is wrong because 54 is the decimal value, and in octal (54)₈ = 44.
